examples.6.1 Technical vision and constraints: Moonshift runs at 60 fps on a GTX 1060 laptop, loads Hadley Depot in 8 seconds, holds 200 interactive props, and saves in under 2 seconds; a clean checkout builds in 25 minutes. The team is 9 people with 3 engineers on Unreal Engine 5.4.2 for 14 months, so the renderer stays stock and networking is out of scope.
examples.6.2 Engine, middleware, and tools: Moonshift pins Unreal Engine 5.4.2 and ships FMOD for adaptive dust-storm audio, Crowdin for six-language string handoff, Steamworks for achievements and cloud saves, and Houdini Engine for the 240-piece habitat kit. Art source lives in Perforce with exclusive checkout; code and tuning tables live in Git, and every plugin has an owner and a removal date.
examples.6.3 Platforms and system requirements: The PC floor is a GTX 1060 with 8 GB RAM at 1080p 60 fps on High; Steam Deck targets 800p 40 fps on Medium, and the console build targets 4K 60 fps on Performance. The build installs at 18 GB, first load is 45 seconds cold, and every subsequent level load stays under 8 seconds.
examples.6.4 Architecture and modules: Core owns boot, time, and logging; Data owns schemas and validation; Gameplay owns repair rules and progression; World owns streaming and navigation; UI and Audio consume events and never write state. The frame runs input, gameplay in fixed 30 Hz steps, physics, animation, then UI and audio, and the build graph reports zero cycles.
examples.6.5 Data model and save format: The save stores Player with inventory and position, World with seed and actor states, Quest with stage and counters, Settings, and Profile in a versioned binary with a build ID. Version 7 migrates one step at a time, writes to a temp file then renames, keeps one backup slot, and resolves cloud conflicts by playtime with a player choice under 10 minutes.
examples.6.6 Networking and multiplayer: Moonshift ships single-player only: the client owns the simulation, saves are local, and no gameplay code assumes a network. If co-op were added, the host would be server-authoritative at 30 Hz with client prediction and rollback, friends-only lobbies, a 150 ms playable latency budget, and full offline campaign play.
examples.6.7 Performance budgets: Hadley Depot must hold 8 ms CPU and 11 ms GPU at 1080p High, 6 GB memory, 1,800 draw calls, an 8-second level load, and 3 hours on Steam Deck. The team captures every Friday on the minimum spec, blocks merges on regressions over 5 percent, and drops resolution scale before shadows, particles, LOD bias, and post-processing.
examples.6.8 Analytics and telemetry: Moonshift logs session_start, level_start, level_end, purchase, and error with build, platform, level, duration, and result, and keeps raw events for 90 days and aggregates for 24 months. The first-run funnel targets 80 percent tutorial completion; consent is asked before the first event, device IDs are salted, and the build never tracks keystrokes, clipboard, or voice audio.
examples.6.9 Build, CI/CD, and QA tooling: Moonshift uses trunk-based development, a commit build that compiles and runs unit tests in under 10 minutes, and a nightly full suite plus performance capture. Release builds are tagged v1.4.2-318, frozen for cert with store metadata and a rollback build, and QA gets dev, QA, staging, and production environments with symbols and a debug teleport menu.
examples.6.10 Security, cheating, and live operat: The threat model covers save editing, memory editing, leaked CI keys, and replay tampering; saves carry checksums, competitive values would be server-authoritative, and build keys rotate every 30 days. Hotfixes ship within 24 hours of a blocker, content patches every 6 weeks, and a rollback drill runs each milestone against a 2 percent crash-rate trigger.
